Photon (Spectrum)

Bring agents to any interface.

Photon (photon.codes) builds Spectrum, a multi-channel agent framework that makes AI agents reachable over real conversation surfaces like iMessage, SMS, and email instead of trapping them in web chat.

## About Photon **[Photon](https://photon.codes)** builds infrastructure for AI agents that operate over real communication channels. Spectrum is Photon’s open-source multi-channel agent framework, enabling AI agents to communicate through interfaces people already use—such as iMessage, SMS, email, Slack, Discord, and voice—instead of being confined to web chat. Learn more at **https://photon.codes**. ## Getting Started The fastest way to ship is with **Spectrum Cloud** — hosted infrastructure for platforms like iMessage, with credentials ready in minutes. 1. Sign up at **[app.photon.codes](https://app.photon.codes)** to get your project ID and secret. 2. Install the SDK (`spectrum-ts` is batteries-included — the runtime plus the standard provider set): ```bash bun add spectrum-ts ``` 3. Start your app: ```typescript import { Spectrum } from "spectrum-ts"; import { imessage } from "spectrum-ts/providers/imessage"; const app = await Spectrum({ projectId: process.env.PROJECT_ID, projectSecret: process.env.PROJECT_SECRET, providers: [imessage.config()], }); for await (const [space, message] of app.messages) { await space.responding(async () => { await message.reply("Hello from Spectrum."); }); } ``` Spectrum also runs fully standalone — you can connect to a local iMessage database with the separate [`@spectrum-ts/imessage-local`](https://npmjs.com/package/@spectrum-ts/imessage-local) package, bring your own gRPC endpoints, or build your own platform provider. See the [docs](https://docs.photon.codes) for self-hosted setups. ## Documentation Visit **[docs.photon.codes](https://docs.photon.codes)** to view the full documentation. ## Platforms | Platform | Package | |----------|---------| | iMessage | [`@spectrum-ts/imessage`](https://npmjs.com/package/@spectrum-ts/imessage) | | Local iMessage | [`@spectrum-ts/imessage-local`](https://npmjs.com/package/@spectrum-ts/imessage-local) (explicit install only) | | WhatsApp Business | [`@spectrum-ts/whatsapp-business`](https://npmjs.com/package/@spectrum-ts/whatsapp-business) | | Telegram | [`@spectrum-ts/telegram`](https://npmjs.com/package/@spectrum-ts/telegram) | | Slack | [`@spectrum-ts/slack`](https://npmjs.com/package/@spectrum-ts/slack) | | Terminal | [`@spectrum-ts/terminal`](https://npmjs.com/package/@spectrum-ts/terminal) | | Custom | `definePlatform` from `spectrum-ts` | `bun add spectrum-ts` is batteries-included (the standard provider set; local iMessage is an explicit install). For a smaller install, depend on the runtime plus only the providers you use — `bun add @spectrum-ts/core @spectrum-ts/telegram` — and import from the scoped packages directly. Either way the `spectrum-ts/providers/` import paths work as long as the matching provider package is installed; if it isn't, the import fails at build/startup naming the exact package to add. ## Issues Found a bug or have a feature request? Please [open an issue](https://github.com/photon-hq/spectrum-ts/issues) on GitHub. Before filing, search existing issues to avoid duplicates. ## Contributing Contributions are welcome. Please read [CONTRIBUTING.md](./CONTRIBUTING.md) for details on our code of conduct and the process for submitting pull requests. ## License [MIT](./LICENSE) © [Photon](https://photon.codes) ---AGENTS--- # Ultracite Code Standards This project uses **Ultracite**, a zero-config preset that enforces strict code quality standards through automated formatting and linting. ## Quick Reference - **Format code**: `bun x ultracite fix` - **Check for issues**: `bun x ultracite check` - **Diagnose setup**: `bun x ultracite doctor` Biome (the underlying engine) provides robust linting and formatting. Most issues are automatically fixable. --- ## Core Principles Write code that is **accessible, performant, type-safe, and maintainable**. Focus on clarity and explicit intent over brevity. ### Type Safety & Explicitness - Use explicit types for function parameters and return values when they enhance clarity - Prefer `unknown` over `any` when the type is genuinely unknown - Use const assertions (`as const`) for immutable values and literal types - Leverage TypeScript's type narrowing instead of type assertions - Use meaningful variable names instead of magic numbers - extract constants with descriptive names ### Modern JavaScript/TypeScript - Use arrow functions for callbacks and short functions - Prefer `for...of` loops over `.forEach()` and indexed `for` loops - Use optional chaining (`?.`) and nullish coalescing (`??`) for safer property access - Prefer template literals over string concatenation - Use destructuring for object and array assignments - Use `const` by default, `let` only when reassignment is needed, never `var` ### Async & Promises - Always `await` promises in async functions - don't forget to use the return value - Use `async/await` syntax instead of promise chains for better readability - Handle errors appropriately in async code with try-catch blocks - Don't use async functions as Promise executors ### React & JSX - Use function components over class components - Call hooks at the top level only, never conditionally - Specify all dependencies in hook dependency arrays correctly - Use the `key` prop for elements in iterables (prefer unique IDs over array indices) - Nest children between opening and closing tags instead of passing as props - Don't define components inside other components - Use semantic HTML and ARIA attributes for accessibility: - Provide meaningful alt text for images - Use proper heading hierarchy - Add labels for form inputs - Include keyboard event handlers alongside mouse events - Use semantic elements (`

Public Mintlify documentation for `spectrum-ts`, authored here next to the code
and rendered by the [photon-hq/docs](https://github.com/photon-hq/docs)

  Practices, and Troubleshooting.

--- title: Inbound pipeline description: Debouncing message bursts, batching, and surviving cancellation without dropping messages. --- People text in bursts. A real conversation looks like this: ``` hey wait actually do you know if the train runs on holidays ``` Four messages in eight seconds. If your agent fires a generation on each one, you get four overlapping replies - and the model never sees the actual question. The fix is to debounce: wait a few seconds for the burst to settle, and handle whatever has accumulated as one turn. ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant U as User participant Q as Batch queue participant H as Batch handler U->>Q: "hey" Q->>Q: schedule flush in 5s U->>Q: "wait" Q->>Q: reset flush timer U->>Q: "actually" Q->>Q: reset flush timer U->>Q: "do you know..." Q->>Q: reset flush timer Note over Q: 5s elapse, no new message Q->>H: flush - drain all four messages H->>H: generate one reply ``` A few seconds of fixed debounce gets you most of the way there. The harder problems are what happens after the flush. ## Drain in the handler, not the enqueuer The single most important rule: **the messages stay in the queue table until the handler reads them.** Don't pull them into the job payload at enqueue time. Why: if the batch-flush job gets cancelled before the handler runs, anything in the payload is lost. Anything still in the queue is naturally picked up by the next batch. Keeping the data in the queue table until the last possible moment makes cancellation a non-event for those messages. ```mermaid flowchart TD A[New message] --> B[Insert into batch_queue table] B --> C{Batch flush job
already scheduled?} C -->|yes| D[Reset its run_at to now + debounce] C -->|no| E[Schedule new batch flush job] D --> F[Job fires at run_at] E --> F F --> G[Handler reads + deletes rows
from batch_queue] G --> H[Hand drained messages to read stage] ``` If the flush job is cancelled between steps F and G, the rows stay in `batch_queue` and the next incoming message picks them up. ## Carry-forward Sometimes the handler does drain the queue but is then cancelled mid-generation. Those messages are now in memory inside a cancelled job - they'd be lost on the floor. The fix is a `carried_messages` table. When a job is cancelled after draining, write the drained messages there. The next batch's handler reads from `carried_messages` first and prepends them as `[Earlier message] ...` lines so the model sees them as historical context, not as fresh input. ```mermaid stateDiagram-v2 [*] --> Queued Queued --> Drained: handler starts Drained --> Generating: pass to LLM Generating --> Sent: reply complete Generating --> Carried: cancelled Carried --> Queued: re-enqueued for next batch Sent --> [*] ``` ## In-flight cancellation When a new message arrives and you have a job in flight (reading, generating, or sending), you need to stop it. Two pieces: 1. **A cancellation flag** in a per-chat `in_flight` table. The enqueuer sets `cancelled_at` and calls `boss.cancel(jobId)`. 2. **Polling inside the handler.** The send stage in particular polls `cancelled_at` every 500ms and aborts via an `AbortController`. The subtle bit: compare `cancelled_at` against the chain's own `chainStartedAt` timestamp, not against "is the flag set." Otherwise a stale flag from a prior cancelled chain orphans the new one. The flag is per-chain, not per-chat. ```ts const inflight = await readInflight(chatId); if (inflight?.cancelled_at && inflight.cancelled_at > chainStartedAt) { abortController.abort(); } ``` ## What you give up This pipeline buys you correctness at the cost of a few hundred milliseconds of hop latency between stages. For a conversational Spectrum agent that's irrelevant - humans don't notice 300ms when a "real" reply takes 5 seconds anyway. For a low-latency tool integration, you'd consolidate stages. =====ARCH===== --- title: Architecture description: Patterns for building human-feeling agents on Spectrum --- This is the architecture we use at Photon to ship agents that **live natively inside IM apps**. The patterns below are pulled directly from production, based on the problems we encountered and the solutions we built to solve them. They're not theoretical best practices - they're the ones that **worked in the real world, with real users, and real bugs**. If you're building a similar agent, these patterns will save you **months** of trial and error. A naive Spectrum agent - read incoming, call the LLM, send the reply - falls apart in ways you don't see until you ship it. The user types "hey" → "wait" → "actually nvm" inside three seconds and gets three independent responses. The agent replies in 200ms when a real person would take five minutes. A worker crashes mid-send and the user receives the same message twice on retry. This section captures the patterns that solve those problems, drawn from production agents built on Spectrum. ## The pipeline Every incoming message flows through five stages backed by a job queue. Each stage is a separately enqueued job, which is what makes any of them cancellable when a follow-up message lands. ```mermaid flowchart LR In([Incoming message]) --> BQ[(Batch queue)] BQ -->|debounce window| Flush[Batch flush] Flush --> Read[Mark as read] Read --> Gen[Generate reply] Gen --> Send[Send with pacing] Send --> Done([Done]) Inflight[(In-flight table)] -.tracks.- Flush Inflight -.tracks.- Read Inflight -.tracks.- Gen Inflight -.tracks.- Send ``` The `In-flight` table is a per-chat record of whichever job ID currently owns each stage. When a new message arrives, the enqueuer reads it, cancels those jobs, and moves any messages that were already drained into a carry-forward table so the next batch sees them. ## Why split it up If you do everything in one handler - read, generate, send - you lose the ability to react to a new message that arrives during generation. By the time you notice, you've already sent a reply that ignored what the user just said, or you've raced the LLM against itself. Splitting into stages costs a few hundred ms of extra hop latency and buys you: - **Cancellation points.** Each stage can check a flag and abort cleanly. - **Resume points.** A worker crash mid-stage retries one stage, not the whole conversation turn. - **Idempotency seams.** The send stage carries stable client GUIDs so retries don't double-send. - **Distinct timing.** The read stage can sleep for an hour while the send stage runs in 500ms - they're independent jobs. ## What's in this section - [Inbound pipeline](/best-practices/inbound-pipeline) - debouncing message bursts, batching, surviving cancellation, and the carry-forward rule that keeps messages from getting lost. - [Recovery and state](/best-practices/recovery-and-state) - idempotent retries via client GUIDs, per-resource memory scope, and a durable failure audit log.

Is Web Crypto (crypto.subtle) available? What are the time/CPU limits for actions in each runtime? Can HTTP actions use the Node runtime ("use node")?

result.output:
# Convex Runtime Comparison

## Default (V8) Runtime vs Node.js Runtime

The default Convex runtime is a "custom JavaScript runtime very similar to the Cloudflare Workers runtime" with no cold starts and web standard APIs. The Node.js runtime is an opt-in alternative available only for actions via the `"use node"` directive.

## Available APIs in Default Runtime

The default runtime supports:
- **Network APIs**: fetch (actions only), Blob, File, FormData, Headers, Request, Response
- **Encoding APIs**: TextEncoder, TextDecoder, atob, btoa
- **Web Streams**: ReadableStream, WritableStream, TransformStream, etc.
- **Web Crypto**: the `crypto` object with SubtleCrypto
- **Timing**: performance.now(), Performance APIs
- **Limited Node APIs**: process.env, AsyncLocalStorage, AsyncResource

## Node Built-in Modules

Node.js modules like `node:crypto` and `node:http2` are **not available** in the default runtime. However, "Web Crypto APIs" including the standard `crypto` object are supported, providing cryptographic functionality.

## Time/CPU Limits

The document does not specify time or CPU limits for either runtime.

## Node.js Runtime for HTTP Actions

Yes, HTTP actions can use the Node.js runtime. Actions are "unrestricted by the same rules of determinism" and can use `"use node"` at the file top to access Node.js features, though this is restricted to actions only.

**Runtime environment:** HTTP actions run in the same environment as queries and mutations, which means they "do not have access to Node.js-specific JavaScript APIs." The documentation does not mention support for "use node" directives in `convex/http.ts`.

**Raw request body and headers:** The second parameter to HTTP action handlers is a standard Fetch API `Request` object. You can access headers via `request.headers` and the body using methods like `.json()`, `.text()`, `.blob()`, or `.arrayBuffer()`.

# Convex Execution and Size Limits

## Execution Time Limits

**Convex Runtime Actions:** "30 minutes"

**Node Runtime Actions:** "10 minutes"

**Queries and Mutations:** "1 second" - this applies only to user code and excludes database operations.

**HTTP Actions:** Follow the same execution time constraints as their respective runtime type.

## Scheduling and Function Limits

**Scheduled Functions:** A single mutation can schedule up to "1000" other functions. The system supports "1,000,000" outstanding scheduled functions overall.

**Scheduled Function Arguments:** Individual arguments are capped at "4 MiB", with a total limit of "16 MiB" for all arguments scheduled in a single mutation.

## Size Constraints

**Function Arguments:** Convex runtime actions support up to "16 MiB", though Node actions are restricted to "5MiB".

**Function Return Values:** Limited to "16 MiB" across all deployment types.

**Document Size:** Each document cannot exceed "1 MiB" and is subject to nested object restrictions including "16" levels of field nesting depth and "1024" maximum fields per document.

# Convex Twilio Component Overview

## Tables
The component owns a `messages` table that stores both sent and received SMS records, including message metadata and delivery status.

## Inbound Webhooks
Webhook registration occurs through `twilio.registerRoutes(http)` in an `http.ts` file. This call "registers the routes necessary for the component," creating two endpoints:

- `YOUR_CONVEX_SITE_URL/twilio/message-status` - tracks delivery status of outbound messages
- `YOUR_CONVEX_SITE_URL/twilio/incoming-message` - captures inbound messages to your Twilio number

A custom `httpPrefix` option allows routing to alternative paths.

## Outbound Sends
The `sendMessage()` action sends SMS via the Twilio API. Messages accept `to` and `body` parameters, with an optional `defaultFrom` phone number configured during instantiation.

## Client Class API
The `Twilio` class provides:
- **Send**: `sendMessage(ctx, {to, body})`
- **Query**: `list()`, `listIncoming()`, `listOutgoing()`, `getMessageBySid()`, `getMessagesTo()`, `getMessagesFrom()`, `getMessagesByCounterparty()`
- **Callbacks**: `incomingMessageCallback` for custom logic on received messages
- **Registration**: `registerIncomingSmsHandler()` to associate webhooks with Twilio phone numbers

## Node Runtime
The documentation does not explicitly mention Node.js runtime usage.

Based on the search results, here's information about `createFunctionHandle` in Convex:

## Overview

createFunctionHandle creates a serializable reference to a Convex function. Passing this reference to another component allows that component to call this function during the current function execution or at any later time.

## Usage Pattern

If you have a valid function reference, you can turn it into something that can be called from anywhere using `const handle = await createFunctionHandle(api.foo.bar)`, and this handle is a string.

## Callback Use Cases

When the app needs to pass a callback function to the component, function handles are used. This is common for components that run app-defined logic on a schedule or in a workflow.

## Best Practices

You should use createFunctionHandle(api.foo.bar) to pass callbacks across boundaries. Handles are strings; use v.string() validators and cast back to FunctionHandle.

# Convex component for Spectrum iMessage

## Context

Convex apps can't run Spectrum's primary integration mode: `for await (… of app.messages)` needs a long-lived process, and Convex only offers request-scoped functions. The existing escape hatch — `app.webhook()` + the hono/express/fastify adapters — doesn't fit Convex either:

- `app.webhook()`'s handler is **fire-and-forget after the response**, which the core docs themselves warn is unsafe on serverless ("enqueue and process in a separate worker"). Convex *is* that worker — but users have to hand-roll it.
- Core's HMAC verify (`packages/core/src/webhook/verify.ts`) uses `node:crypto`; Convex's default V8 runtime has no Node builtins (only Web Crypto).
- Outbound iMessage goes over gRPC (`@photon-ai/advanced-imessage` → `nice-grpc`/`@grpc/grpc-js`), which only works in Convex's `"use node"` actions.
- Everything `docs/best-practices/` says a production agent needs — burst debouncing, batch queue, in-flight cancellation, carry-forward, idempotent paced sends — maps 1:1 onto Convex primitives (tables, `ctx.scheduler`, transactional mutations) and should be shipped, not documented.

**Deliverable:** a Convex component `@spectrum-ts/convex` in a **new repo** (`photon-hq/spectrum-convex`) that gives Convex apps first-class Spectrum iMessage support with the production pipeline built in, plus small companion changes in this repo (portable webhook primitives, remote-API export, docs page).

## Decisions (confirmed with user)

1. **Send transport:** gRPC now via a `"use node"` action, hidden behind an internal `Sender` interface so a REST/fetch transport can replace it later without public API changes.
2. **Scope:** full pipeline component from day one (debounce → flush → cancel/carry-forward → idempotent paced send), not just a webhook adapter.
3. **Location:** separate repo, following the `get-convex/*` component template (e.g. `get-convex/twilio`). Companion changes land in this monorepo.

## Architecture

### Inbound (V8 runtime, no Node deps)

```
Spectrum Cloud ──native webhook POST──▶ https://<deployment>.convex.site/spectrum/webhook
  └─ app-context httpAction (from spectrum.registerRoutes(http)):
       read raw bytes once → HMAC verify (Web Crypto) → zod slim-envelope parse
       → ctx.runMutation(components.spectrum.inbound.enqueue, …) → 200
```

- **Native Spectrum webhook only** (normalized JSON + `webhookSecret`). No fusor path — it needs protobuf decode + a fusor provider and adds nothing on Convex.
- The httpAction lives in **app context** (Twilio-component pattern) so it can read `process.env.SPECTRUM_WEBHOOK_SECRET`; the component itself declares env vars for project credentials (see Sender).
- Durable enqueue-before-200 **replaces** core's fire-and-forget dispatch — strictly better on serverless.

### Pipeline (component tables + scheduler; mirrors `docs/best-practices/`)

Tables (component-isolated):

| Table | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `inbound` | every verified envelope; **dedupe on message id** (webhook is at-least-once); doubles as batch queue via `status: queued → drained → handled` |
| `spaces` | registry: spaceId → phone, type, lastInboundAt (routing info for sends) |
| `inflight` | per space: flush/handler `_scheduled_functions` ids, `chainStartedAt`, `cancelledAt` |
| `carried` | drained-but-cancelled messages, prepended to the next batch (carry-forward rule) |
| `outbox` | sends with deterministic `clientGuid` (chainId+index) for idempotency, pacing state, status/attempts audit |

Flow:

1. `enqueue` (mutation): dedupe insert → upsert space → cancel current chain (`ctx.scheduler.cancel` on flush/handler jobs, set `cancelledAt`, move drained rows to `carried`) → cancel+reschedule `flush` at `debounceMs` (Convex's version of "reset run_at").
2. `flush` (internal mutation): drain `carried` + `queued` rows (messages stay in the table until here — the "drain in the handler" rule), stamp `chainStartedAt`, schedule the **app's batch handler** via a function handle (`createFunctionHandle(options.onBatch)`, threaded through enqueue args).
3. App handler (user's `internalAction`): gets `{ space, messages, carried, chainId }`, calls their LLM, replies through the client class.
4. **Cooperative cancellation:** `ctx.scheduler.cancel` can't kill an already-running action, so — exactly as `docs/best-practices/inbound-pipeline.mdx.vel` prescribes — the component exposes `isCancelled(chainId)` (compares `cancelledAt > chainStartedAt`) and the `send` mutation rejects writes from a cancelled chain. The client-class helpers check it automatically between steps.
5. `outbox.enqueue` (mutation) → schedules the Node sender per item with pacing delays (`runAfter`); retries by rescheduling with backoff, status transitions recorded.

### Outbound (Node runtime, behind `Sender`)

- One `"use node"` component action wraps the gRPC client: send/reply/edit/unsend, tapbacks, typing, markRead, getAttachment.
- Internal interface `Sender { sendText; reply; react; edit; unsend; markRead; typing; getAttachment; … }` — the gRPC implementation is the only one now; a REST implementation slots in later.
- Reuses this repo's existing code via the companion export (below): `createCloudClients` (token mint + rotation, `packages/imessage/src/auth.ts`) and the aggregated remote API (`packages/imessage/src/remote/api.ts`), with a module-level client cache for Lambda warm starts.
- Credentials via **component env vars** (`defineComponent` typed env declaration): `SPECTRUM_PROJECT_ID` / `SPECTRUM_PROJECT_SECRET` — never passed as function args.
- Inbound attachments: slim webhook carries metadata only; `fetchAttachment(ctx, attachmentId)` node action pulls bytes over gRPC and stores them in **Convex file storage**, returning a storage id.

### Public API (app-side client class)

```ts
// convex/convex.config.ts
import spectrum from "@spectrum-ts/convex/convex.config";
app.use(spectrum);

// convex/spectrum.ts
export const spectrum = new Spectrum(components.spectrum, {
  onBatch: internal.agent.respond,
  debounceMs: 5000,
  pacing: { perMessageMs: 800 },
  autoMarkRead: true,
});

// convex/http.ts
spectrum.registerRoutes(http); // POST /spectrum/webhook

// convex/agent.ts
export const respond = spectrum.batchHandler(async (ctx, batch) => {
  // batch.messages / batch.carried; helpers bound to chainId:
  await batch.reply("…");   // → outbox, rejected if chain cancelled
});
```

Plus: `spectrum.send(ctx, spaceId, content)`, `react`, `markRead`, `fetchAttachment`, and queries (`listMessages`, `getSpace`) for dashboards.

## Repos and file layout

### New repo `photon-hq/spectrum-convex` (package `@spectrum-ts/convex`)

Follow the get-convex component template:

```
src/component/   convex.config.ts, schema.ts, inbound.ts, pipeline.ts, outbox.ts,
                 sender.node.ts ("use node"), _generated/
src/client/      index.ts (Spectrum class, registerRoutes, batchHandler)
src/shared/      wire types re-exported from @spectrum-ts/core/webhook
example/         runnable Convex app (echo agent) used for dev + e2e
```

package.json exports: `.`, `./convex.config.js`, `./_generated/component.js`; codegen via `npx convex codegen --component-dir src/component`.

### Companion changes in this repo (`spectrum-ts`)

1. **Portable webhook primitives — `@spectrum-ts/core/webhook` subpath.**
   - Rewrite `packages/core/src/webhook/verify.ts` on Web Crypto (`crypto.subtle`, async; use `subtle.verify` for constant-time compare). Works on Node ≥ 18.17 / Bun / V8 isolates. Update the one internal call site (`handleSpectrumWebhook` in `packages/core/src/spectrum.ts` — already async) and `packages/core/test/webhook/verify.test.ts`.
   - New entry `packages/core/src/webhook/index.ts` exporting `verifySpectrumSignature` + the slim zod schemas from `webhook/types.ts` (already dependency-free). **Exclude** `deserialize.ts` (pulls `node:fs`/`node:crypto` via content builders).
   - Add the `./webhook` subpath to `packages/core/package.json` exports (pattern: existing `./authoring` subpath).
2. **Remote API export — `@spectrum-ts/imessage/remote` subpath** exposing the existing aggregation module `packages/imessage/src/remote/api.ts` plus `createCloudClients`/`disposeCloudAuth` from `src/auth.ts` and the routing helpers in `src/remote/client.ts`. Node-only by design; no new logic.
3. **Docs:** `docs/integrations/convex.mdx.vel` (install, config, pipeline semantics, cancellation contract) + entry in `docs/nav.json` Integrations group.

## Implementation phases

- **Phase 0 (this repo):** companion changes 1–2 + tests. Ship as a normal minor release so the new repo can depend on published versions.
- **Phase 1:** scaffold new repo (component template, codegen, CI, example app).
- **Phase 2:** inbound — `registerRoutes`, Web Crypto verify, `enqueue` with dedupe + space registry.
- **Phase 3:** pipeline — debounce flush, inflight/cancel/carry-forward, function-handle dispatch, `isCancelled`.
- **Phase 4:** outbound — outbox, pacing, gRPC `Sender` node action, typing/read/tapbacks, chain-guarded `send`.
- **Phase 5:** attachments → Convex storage; dashboard queries; failure audit fields.
- **Phase 6:** docs page in this repo, README, publish.

## Verification

- **This repo:** `bun run check && bun run typecheck && bun run test` (verify tests updated for async verify; everything else must pass unchanged).
- **New repo unit tests** (`convex-test` + vitest): signed-fixture verify (port the tiny `signSpectrum` helper from `packages/test-support/src/webhook.ts` — it's workspace-private); enqueue dedupe; debounce reset (cancel+reschedule); cancellation moves drained rows to `carried`; next flush prepends carried; outbox clientGuid idempotency; cancelled-chain `send` rejection.
- **e2e:** `example/` app on `npx convex dev` — script POSTs a signed native-webhook envelope to the local site URL, assert batch handler fires once per burst and outbox rows transition to `sent` (sender mocked); then a live smoke test against a Spectrum Cloud sandbox line.

## Risks / open items

- **grpc-js bundling inside a component's node action**: the Mastra component proves node-in-component works but needed an app-side `"use node"` workaround file for bundling. Fallback (isolated behind `Sender`): ship the sender as an app-side re-export (`export const sender = makeSenderAction()` in a user `"use node"` file) wired via function handle. The REST-transport future removes this class of problem entirely.
- **Already-running actions can't be force-cancelled** — mitigated by the cooperative `chainId` contract, which is the same trade-off the best-practices docs already made.
- Convex limits are comfortable: 20 MiB http bodies vs. small slim envelopes; 1 MiB docs vs. metadata-only attachments (bytes go to file storage); node actions 10 min.

# Convex component for Spectrum iMessage

## Context

Convex apps can't run Spectrum's primary integration mode: `for await (… of app.messages)` needs a long-lived process, and Convex only offers request-scoped functions. The existing escape hatch — `app.webhook()` + the hono/express/fastify adapters — doesn't fit Convex either:

- `app.webhook()`'s handler is **fire-and-forget after the response**, which the core docs themselves warn is unsafe on serverless ("enqueue and process in a separate worker"). Convex *is* that worker — but users have to hand-roll it.
- Core's HMAC verify (`packages/core/src/webhook/verify.ts`) uses `node:crypto`; Convex's default V8 runtime has no Node builtins (only Web Crypto).
- Outbound iMessage goes over gRPC (`@photon-ai/advanced-imessage` → `nice-grpc`/`@grpc/grpc-js`), which only works in Convex's `"use node"` actions.
- Everything `docs/best-practices/` says a production agent needs — burst debouncing, batch queue, in-flight cancellation, carry-forward, idempotent paced sends — maps 1:1 onto Convex primitives (tables, `ctx.scheduler`, transactional mutations) and should be shipped, not documented.

**Deliverable:** a Convex component `@spectrum-ts/convex` in a **new repo** (`photon-hq/spectrum-convex`) that gives Convex apps first-class Spectrum iMessage support with the production pipeline built in, plus small companion changes in this repo (portable webhook primitives, remote-API export, docs page).

## Decisions (confirmed with user)

1. **Send transport:** gRPC now via a `"use node"` action, hidden behind an internal `Sender` interface so a REST/fetch transport can replace it later without public API changes.
2. **Scope:** full pipeline component from day one (debounce → flush → cancel/carry-forward → idempotent paced send), not just a webhook adapter.
3. **Location:** separate repo, following the `get-convex/*` component template (e.g. `get-convex/twilio`). Companion changes land in this monorepo.

## Architecture

### Inbound (V8 runtime, no Node deps)

```
Spectrum Cloud ──native webhook POST──▶ https://<deployment>.convex.site/spectrum/webhook
  └─ app-context httpAction (from spectrum.registerRoutes(http)):
       read raw bytes once → HMAC verify (Web Crypto) → zod slim-envelope parse
       → ctx.runMutation(components.spectrum.inbound.enqueue, …) → 200
```

- **Native Spectrum webhook only** (normalized JSON + `webhookSecret`). No fusor path — it needs protobuf decode + a fusor provider and adds nothing on Convex.
- The httpAction lives in **app context** (Twilio-component pattern) so it can read `process.env.SPECTRUM_WEBHOOK_SECRET`; the component itself declares env vars for project credentials (see Sender).
- Durable enqueue-before-200 **replaces** core's fire-and-forget dispatch — strictly better on serverless.

### Pipeline (component tables + scheduler; mirrors `docs/best-practices/`)

Tables (component-isolated):

| Table | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `inbound` | every verified envelope; **dedupe on message id** (webhook is at-least-once); doubles as batch queue via `status: queued → drained → handled` |
| `spaces` | registry: spaceId → phone, type, lastInboundAt (routing info for sends) |
| `inflight` | per space: flush/handler `_scheduled_functions` ids, `chainStartedAt`, `cancelledAt` |
| `carried` | drained-but-cancelled messages, prepended to the next batch (carry-forward rule) |
| `outbox` | sends with deterministic `clientGuid` (chainId+index) for idempotency, pacing state, status/attempts audit |

Flow:

1. `enqueue` (mutation): dedupe insert → upsert space → cancel current chain (`ctx.scheduler.cancel` on flush/handler jobs, set `cancelledAt`, move drained rows to `carried`) → cancel+reschedule `flush` at `debounceMs` (Convex's version of "reset run_at").
2. `flush` (internal mutation): drain `carried` + `queued` rows (messages stay in the table until here — the "drain in the handler" rule), stamp `chainStartedAt`, schedule the **app's batch handler** via a function handle (`createFunctionHandle(options.onBatch)`, threaded through enqueue args).
3. App handler (user's `internalAction`): gets `{ space, messages, carried, chainId }`, calls their LLM, replies through the client class.
4. **Cooperative cancellation:** `ctx.scheduler.cancel` can't kill an already-running action, so — exactly as `docs/best-practices/inbound-pipeline.mdx.vel` prescribes — the component exposes `isCancelled(chainId)` (compares `cancelledAt > chainStartedAt`) and the `send` mutation rejects writes from a cancelled chain. The client-class helpers check it automatically between steps.
5. `outbox.enqueue` (mutation) → schedules the Node sender per item with pacing delays (`runAfter`); retries by rescheduling with backoff, status transitions recorded.

### Outbound (Node runtime, behind `Sender`)

- One `"use node"` component action wraps the gRPC client: send/reply/edit/unsend, tapbacks, typing, markRead, getAttachment.
- Internal interface `Sender { sendText; reply; react; edit; unsend; markRead; typing; getAttachment; … }` — the gRPC implementation is the only one now; a REST implementation slots in later.
- Reuses this repo's existing code via the companion export (below): `createCloudClients` (token mint + rotation, `packages/imessage/src/auth.ts`) and the aggregated remote API (`packages/imessage/src/remote/api.ts`), with a module-level client cache for Lambda warm starts.
- Credentials via **component env vars** (`defineComponent` typed env declaration): `SPECTRUM_PROJECT_ID` / `SPECTRUM_PROJECT_SECRET` — never passed as function args.
- Inbound attachments: slim webhook carries metadata only; `fetchAttachment(ctx, attachmentId)` node action pulls bytes over gRPC and stores them in **Convex file storage**, returning a storage id.

### Public API (app-side client class)

```ts
// convex/convex.config.ts
import spectrum from "@spectrum-ts/convex/convex.config";
app.use(spectrum);

// convex/spectrum.ts
export const spectrum = new Spectrum(components.spectrum, {
  onBatch: internal.agent.respond,
  debounceMs: 5000,
  pacing: { perMessageMs: 800 },
  autoMarkRead: true,
});

// convex/http.ts
spectrum.registerRoutes(http); // POST /spectrum/webhook

// convex/agent.ts
export const respond = spectrum.batchHandler(async (ctx, batch) => {
  // batch.messages / batch.carried; helpers bound to chainId:
  await batch.reply("…");   // → outbox, rejected if chain cancelled
});
```

Plus: `spectrum.send(ctx, spaceId, content)`, `react`, `markRead`, `fetchAttachment`, and queries (`listMessages`, `getSpace`) for dashboards.

input.content:
import { defineSchema, defineTable } from "convex/server";
import { v } from "convex/values";

/**
 * Slim inbound content, stored exactly as the native Spectrum webhook
 * delivered it. Kept as an opaque `v.any()` rather than a discriminated union
 * on purpose: the webhook wire format is additive (new content arms ship
 * without an SDK bump), and a strict validator here would reject a delivery
 * the SDK itself is happy to parse. Narrowing happens in app code, where the
 * `Content` types from `@spectrum-ts/core` apply.
 */
const slimContent = v.any();

export const inboundStatus = v.union(
  // Waiting for a flush to pick it up.
  v.literal("queued"),
  // Handed to a batch; still owned by a live chain.
  v.literal("drained"),
  // The chain that drained it completed.
  v.literal("handled")
);

export const outboxStatus = v.union(
  v.literal("pending"),
  v.literal("sending"),
  v.literal("sent"),
  v.literal("failed"),
  // The chain that queued this send was superseded before it went out.
  v.literal("cancelled")
);

export default defineSchema({
  /**
   * Every verified inbound message, and the batch queue itself. Messages stay
   * here until a flush drains them — the "drain in the handler, not the
   * enqueuer" rule — so a cancelled flush loses nothing.
   */
  inbound: defineTable({
    spaceId: v.string(),
    // Provider message id. Native webhooks are at-least-once, so this is the
    // dedupe key.
    messageId: v.string(),
    platform: v.string(),
    senderId: v.optional(v.string()),
    content: slimContent,
    // Wire timestamp (ISO 8601) as delivered; `receivedAt` is our clock.
    timestamp: v.optional(v.string()),
    receivedAt: v.number(),
    status: inboundStatus,
    // Set when a chain drains this row, so cancellation can find its messages.
    chainId: v.optional(v.string()),
    raw: v.optional(v.any()),
  })
    .index("by_message", ["messageId"])
    .index("by_space_status", ["spaceId", "status"])
    .index("by_chain", ["chainId"]),

  /**
   * Routing registry. iMessage sends need the `phone` (which line serves this
   * conversation) and the chat type, neither of which is derivable from the
   * space id alone in multi-line mode.
   */
  spaces: defineTable({
    spaceId: v.string(),
    platform: v.string(),
    phone: v.optional(v.string()),
    type: v.optional(v.union(v.literal("dm"), v.literal("group"))),
    lastInboundAt: v.number(),
  }).index("by_space", ["spaceId"]),

  /**
   * Per-space record of the chain that currently owns the pipeline. A "chain"
   * is one conversational turn: flush → handler → sends.
   *
   * `ctx.scheduler.cancel` cannot stop an action that has already started, so
   * cancellation is cooperative: `cancelledAt` is compared against the chain's
   * own `chainStartedAt` rather than treated as a boolean, which is what keeps
   * a stale flag from orphaning the chain that replaced it.
   */
  inflight: defineTable({
    spaceId: v.string(),
    chainId: v.optional(v.string()),
    chainStartedAt: v.optional(v.number()),
    cancelledAt: v.optional(v.number()),
    flushJobId: v.optional(v.id("_scheduled_functions")),
    handlerJobId: v.optional(v.id("_scheduled_functions")),
  }).index("by_space", ["spaceId"]),

  /**
   * Messages a cancelled chain had already drained. The next flush prepends
   * them so the model still sees them — as history, not as fresh input.
   */
  carried: defineTable({
    spaceId: v.string(),
    messageId: v.string(),
    content: slimContent,
    senderId: v.optional(v.string()),
    timestamp: v.optional(v.string()),
    carriedAt: v.number(),
  }).index("by_space", ["spaceId"]),

  /**
   * Outbound sends. `clientGuid` is derived deterministically from
   * `(chainId, seq)` and travels to the provider as its idempotency key, so a
   * retried send re-uses the same guid and cannot double-post.
   */
  outbox: defineTable({
    spaceId: v.string(),
    chainId: v.optional(v.string()),
    seq: v.number(),
    clientGuid: v.string(),
    kind: v.union(
      v.literal("send"),
      v.literal("reply"),
      v.literal("react"),
      v.literal("markRead"),
      v.literal("typing")
    ),
    content: v.optional(slimContent),
    targetMessageId: v.optional(v.string()),
    reaction: v.optional(v.string()),
    status: outboxStatus,
    attempts: v.number(),
    queuedAt: v.number(),
    sentAt: v.optional(v.number()),
    providerMessageId: v.optional(v.string()),
    lastError: v.optional(v.string()),
    jobId: v.optional(v.id("_scheduled_functions")),

import { v } from "convex/values";
import { internalMutation } from "./_generated/server.js";

/**
 * Sender-facing surface.
 *
 * The component deliberately does NOT contain the gRPC client. iMessage sends
 * speak gRPC over HTTP/2, which only Convex's Node runtime can do, and a
 * `"use node"` file cannot host queries or mutations. So the transport lives in
 * an action the *app* owns (see `createSenderAction` in the client package) and
 * the component reaches it through a function handle.
 *
 * That indirection is also the seam the plan calls for: the component depends
 * on the `Sender` contract below, not on gRPC. If Spectrum Cloud grows an HTTPS
 * send endpoint, a fetch-based sender drops in here and the whole pipeline
 * moves to the V8 runtime with no schema or API change.
 */

/** The payload every sender implementation receives. */
export const senderArgs = {
  rowId: v.string(),
  spaceId: v.string(),
  phone: v.optional(v.string()),
  /** Idempotency key — pass through to the provider verbatim. */
  clientGuid: v.string(),
  kind: v.string(),
  content: v.optional(v.any()),
  targetMessageId: v.optional(v.string()),
  reaction: v.optional(v.string()),
};

/**
 * A no-op sender used by tests and by installs that have not wired a transport
 * yet. Marks the row sent without touching the network, so the pipeline can be
 * exercised end to end without a live iMessage line.
 */
export const noopSender = internalMutation({
  args: senderArgs,
  returns: v.null(),
  handler: () => null,
});
EOF

---
title: "eve"
description: "Connect an eve agent to iMessage through Photon"
---

{% set webhookRoute = "/eve/v1/photon" %}
{% set env = {
  projectId: "IMESSAGE_PROJECT_ID",
  projectSecret: "IMESSAGE_PROJECT_SECRET",
  webhookSecret: "IMESSAGE_WEBHOOK_SECRET"
} %}
{% set spectrumInstance = symbol("ts:spectrum-ts#SpectrumInstance") %}
{% set chatMessage = symbol("ts:chat#Message") %}
{% set chatThread = symbol("ts:chat#Thread") %}

[eve](https://vercel.com/eve) can expose an agent over iMessage with
`photonIMessageChannel`. The channel wraps [Photon's Chat SDK iMessage
adapter](https://github.com/photon-hq/vercel-chat-adapter-imessage), which is
built on `spectrum-ts`. You configure an eve channel; you do not need to
construct a Chat SDK `Chat` instance or initialize the underlying
{{ spectrumInstance | typeRef }} yourself.

The channel receives authenticated Photon webhook deliveries at
`{{ webhookRoute }}`, keeps each iMessage conversation in one eve session, and
marks accepted messages as read. If another accepted message arrives while the
agent is replying, it cooperatively cancels the active turn and steers its
replacement instead of starting a second independent reply. Replies are sent
as complete messages rather than token-by-token streams because iMessage does
not support Chat SDK streaming.

This guide covers the Photon side of the integration: provisioning,
credentials, and webhook verification. The channel's TypeScript surface —
imports, configuration options, and callback signatures — is still evolving,
so it is documented upstream in the [eve Photon channel
reference](https://eve.dev/docs/channels/photon) rather than duplicated here.

## Add the Photon channel

If you do not have an eve agent yet, create one first with the
[eve docs](https://eve.dev/docs). From the agent directory, add the Photon
iMessage channel:

```bash
eve add channel/photon-imessage
```

# Example app

A complete Convex app wiring up `@spectrum-ts/convex`: webhook route, batch
handler, Node sender, and attachment storage.

## Run it

```sh
npm install
npx convex dev
```

The first `convex dev` run creates a deployment and generates `convex/_generated/`
for both the app and the component. **Until it has run once, these files
reference modules that don't exist yet**, so the example won't typecheck on a
fresh clone — that's expected, not a broken checkout. It's also why the root
`tsconfig.json` excludes this directory.

Then set the environment variables in the Convex dashboard:

```
SPECTRUM_WEBHOOK_SECRET=whsec_...
SPECTRUM_PROJECT_ID=...
SPECTRUM_PROJECT_SECRET=...
```

and point your Spectrum Cloud webhook at:

```
https://<deployment>.convex.site/spectrum/webhook
```

## What each file does

| File | Role |
|---|---|
| `convex.config.ts` | Installs the component |
| `spectrum.ts` | One shared client; wires `onBatch` and `sender` |
| `http.ts` | Mounts the webhook route |
| `agent.ts` | Batch handler — one invocation per conversational turn |
| `sender.ts` | `"use node"` gRPC transport + attachment storage |

part is the shape around it: re-check `isCancelled` after anything slow, then
`send` and `completeChain`.

Done. Here's my answer to your original question, plus what I built.

## Yes — a component, not just a library

The decisive constraint: `app.webhook()` dispatches its handler **after** the HTTP response, but a Convex isolate freezes the moment you return one. A thin adapter would be structurally broken. The component inverts it — verify and persist *before* the 200, then run everything on Convex's scheduler.

The differentiated value isn't the webhook plumbing, it's that your `docs/best-practices/` pipeline (debounce, cancellation, carry-forward, idempotent paced sends) maps 1:1 onto Convex primitives. Twilio's component gets to be pure-V8 because Twilio has REST; iMessage doesn't, which is why the sender is a `"use node"` action the app owns.

## What's built

**`spectrum-ts` (this repo)** — 32/32 test tasks, 12/12 builds, lint + typecheck clean:
- `packages/core/src/webhook/verify.ts` — rewritten on Web Crypto (now async; `subtle.verify` for constant-time compare). New `@spectrum-ts/core/webhook` subpath exports it plus the slim schemas. `deserialize.ts` is deliberately excluded — it drags in `node:fs`/`node:crypto`.
- `@spectrum-ts/imessage/remote` — curated export of the existing remote API + `createCloudClients`. No new logic.
- `docs/integrations/convex.mdx.vel` + nav entry.

**`../spectrum-convex`** (new repo, git init'd, nothing committed) — 22/22 tests, lint + typecheck + build clean. Component tables/functions, client class, Node sender, example app.

Two places the plan was wrong, both caught by tests:

1. **Timestamp cancellation doesn't work.** `cancelledAt > chainStartedAt` — which your inbound-pipeline doc prescribes — misreads a cancel landing in the same millisecond as its flush as "not cancelled". Now decided by chain identity; `cancelledAt` kept for audit only.
2. **Tapbacks need `{id, content}`.** `reactToMessage` validates via `isMessage`, so the planned bare-id target would have thrown at runtime. The outbox now passes the stored inbound content through.

## Two caveats

- The component repo points `@spectrum-ts/*` at local `file:` paths, since `core/webhook` and `imessage/remote` are unreleased. Restore semver ranges after that minor ships.
- `_generated/` for the component is hand-written from Convex's own codegen templates — `npx convex codegen` requires auth I don't have here. Worth regenerating with `npm run codegen` once you're logged in. Relatedly, `example/` won't typecheck until `npx convex dev` runs once; it's excluded from tsconfig and noted in its README.

The `Sender` interface is the seam that matters long-term: if Spectrum Cloud ever grows an HTTPS send endpoint, a fetch-based implementation drops in and the whole pipeline moves to V8 — which would also unlock Workers, Vercel Edge, and Deno Deploy from the same code.

# Uncrypto Overview

## Exports

Uncrypto exports three main items:

```javascript
// ESM
import { subtle, randomUUID, getRandomValues } from "uncrypto";

// CommonJS
const { subtle, randomUUID, getRandomValues } = require("uncrypto");
```

## Export Conditions

The library leverages "Conditional Exports" to provide platform-specific implementations. It targets both Node.js (using the native Crypto Module) and browsers (using the Web Crypto API), though the specific package.json configuration isn't detailed in the provided content.

## Dependencies

The documentation provided does not list specific package dependencies.

## Node.js Support

According to the requirements section, the library supports **Node.js version 15 and above**. The documentation explicitly states: "this library provides no polyfills for older versions!"

## Additional Requirements

For browser usage, a "Secure Context" (HTTPS or localhost) is required, along with browser support for the SubtleCrypto API. For other runtimes, `globalThis.crypto` and `globalThis.crypto.subtle` must be exposed.

Switched to `uncrypto`. Everything still green: lint, typecheck, 32/32 test tasks, 12/12 builds in the SDK repo; 22/22 tests in the component repo.

## What changed

`packages/core/src/webhook/verify.ts` now does:

```ts
import { subtle } from "uncrypto";
```

replacing the hand-rolled `getSubtle()` that read `globalThis.crypto?.subtle` and threw a runtime error when it was missing. Added `uncrypto@^0.1.3` (zero deps) to `@spectrum-ts/core`.

## Why it's a real improvement, not just a swap

My version had an actual gap: `globalThis.crypto` isn't exposed by default on **Node 18** (it landed as a default global in Node 19). Since `@spectrum-ts/imessage` declares `node >=18.17`, a Node 18 user would have hit that thrown error at webhook-verification time. uncrypto's conditional exports resolve `node` → `node:crypto`'s webcrypto, so the feature check disappears entirely rather than being papered over.

## Verified, not assumed

The thing worth checking was which export condition each runtime picks — resolving `node` inside Convex's V8 isolate would break the inbound path. I bundled the real entry with esbuild using Convex's own settings (`platform: "browser"`, from `convex/dist/cjs/bundler/index.js:247`):

| Bundle target | Resolves to | `node:crypto` refs |
|---|---|---|
| `platform: "browser"` — Convex V8 runtime | `globalThis.crypto` | 0 |
| `platform: "node"` — `"use node"` actions | `node:crypto` webcrypto | 1 |

Also confirmed `import { subtle } from "uncrypto"` survives as an **external** import in core's built chunk (`dist/verify-*.js`), rather than being inlined with the `node` condition at build time — that's what lets the consumer's bundler make the choice. tsdown auto-externalizes `dependencies`, so this works because uncrypto is a real dep, not a bundled one.

content.text:
Tested against a real Convex deployment and live Spectrum Cloud. Both repos green: 32/32 test tasks in the SDK, 23/23 in the component, lint + typecheck + build clean.

## The inbound pipeline works, verified end to end

Deployed the component to a real Convex backend (`✔ Installed component spectrum`) and fired HMAC-signed webhooks at the live HTTP endpoint:

| Behaviour | Result |
|---|---|
| Forged signature | `401 signature-mismatch`, nothing stored |
| Signed delivery | `200`, durable before the response returns |
| Redelivery of a seen id | Deduped — **3 rows from 4 deliveries** |
| Burst of 3 | One flush, one chain, one handler invocation |
| Batch handler | Ran via function handle with `messages` + `carried` |
| Outbound send | Queued as `chat-run4:...#0` — the deterministic guid |
| Send failure | Captured in `lastError`, retried with backoff |

Also confirmed the credentials work: project **NanoClaw**, shared-mode tokens mint, and a live gRPC call returned a real policy error ("Target not allowed for this project") — proving auth, TLS/HTTP2, routing, and error surfacing all work from Node.

## Three bugs only real deployment could find

1. **The component would have shipped broken.** `tsc` doesn't copy `.js`, so `_generated/api.js` and `server.js` never reached `dist/`. Every import unresolvable. Added a copy step.
2. **The documented call pattern threw.** `spectrum.isCancelled(ctx, args)` — what my own README showed — passes the full batch, and Convex rejects extra fields. Every real handler would have died with `ArgumentValidationError`. The client now narrows args; added a regression test.
3. **`@spectrum-ts/imessage` is an optional peer**, so apps using the sender don't get it installed. Documented.

## The finding that changes your design decision

**The gRPC sender cannot work on Convex, and gRPC is no longer the right target anyway.**

`advanced-imessage` guards `createGrpcClient` with `import.meta.resolve()` over three peers. In Convex's bundled Lambda that resolver can't see them as packages, so it throws even when esbuild inlined the code — and `node.externalPackages` doesn't fix it (tested).

Its own error message says: *"The gRPC transport is legacy; new code should use `createHttpClient`, which needs no extra installs."*

I verified that claim: **`createHttpClient`'s entire import graph bundles for `platform: browser` with zero Node builtins, using `fetch`.** It would run natively in Convex's V8 runtime — no `"use node"`, no Node 24, no bundling workarounds. The component collapses to a single runtime.

You picked "gRPC now, REST later" because I told you gRPC was the only option. That was wrong — the HTTP client already exists. The only gap is server-side: the token endpoint returns a bearer token but no HTTP middleware address, and pointing the client at the gRPC host gives `415`. **Once Spectrum Cloud returns that address, this becomes a one-file change** — the `Sender` interface was built for exactly this, so no schema or public API changes.

That's the highest-leverage next step, and it's on the Photon side, not in either repo.

Two notes: nothing is committed in either repo. And those credentials are now in this transcript — worth rotating if it's shared.

content.text:
**Complete success.** The final error is `[spectrum-imessage] Target not allowed for this project` — the exact server-side policy response I got calling gRPC directly from Node. The server authenticated the request, validated the guid, and rejected only because 555-0100 isn't an allowed target.

The full outbound path works on Convex. Let me clean up and correct the docs:

input.command:
cd /Users/qwerzl/Documents/Projects/spectrum-convex && rm -f tmp-e2e.mjs example/convex/probe.ts && python3 - <<'PY'
p = "README.md"
s = open(p).read()
start = s.index("## Sending: current status")
end = s.index("## Verified behaviour")
s = s[:start] + '''## Sending

Sends go through the outbox to a gRPC transport running in a Node action your
app owns. gRPC is the transport for both directions — the SDK's HTTP client has
no `subscribeEvents` / `EventsResource`, so it cannot serve inbound.

Two pieces of setup are required, and **sends fail without them**:

**1. Depend on the provider and the gRPC peers.** `@spectrum-ts/imessage` is an
*optional* peer of this package, so it is not installed for you:

```sh
npm i @spectrum-ts/imessage @photon-ai/advanced-imessage nice-grpc nice-grpc-common @grpc/grpc-js
```

**2. Mark them external, and force-reference the peers.** `createGrpcClient`
requires its peers resolvable at *runtime*, not merely bundled:

```json
// convex.json
{
  "node": {
    "externalPackages": [
      "@photon-ai/advanced-imessage",
      "nice-grpc",
      "nice-grpc-common",
      "@grpc/grpc-js"
    ]
  }
}
```

```ts
// convex/_workaround.ts — nothing imports this; it exists so the packages ship
"use node";
export * as _grpcJs from "@grpc/grpc-js";
export * as _niceGrpc from "nice-grpc";
export * as _niceGrpcCommon from "nice-grpc-common";
```

That second file is not optional. Convex installs an `externalPackages` entry
only if the *bundled code imports it*, and these three are optional peers of
`@photon-ai/advanced-imessage` loaded dynamically from inside that package — so
nothing in the bundle references them and they are silently never installed.
`createGrpcClient` then fails its `import.meta.resolve` check with a misleading
"install the peer dependencies" error even though they are in your
`package.json`. The re-export gives the bundler the static reference it needs.

```ts
// convex/sender.ts
"use node";
import { createCloudSender } from "@spectrum-ts/convex/sender";

const sender = createCloudSender(); // built once per container, not per send
```

<sub>Note: `node.externalPackages` is not honoured by the anonymous local backend
(`CONVEX_AGENT_MODE=anonymous`) — the peers are never installed there regardless

You were right, and testing proved it twice over.

## Outbound gRPC works on Convex — verified against a real cloud deployment

The final send reached Spectrum Cloud and came back with `[spectrum-imessage] Target not allowed for this project` — the *identical* server policy error I got calling gRPC directly from Node. Token mint, TLS, HTTP/2, gRPC, auth, and chat-guid validation all worked; it was rejected only because I used a reserved fictional number (555-0100) as the target.

The progression of errors tells the story:
1. `needs the optional peer dependencies` → peers genuinely absent
2. `chat must start with "any;-;"` → **gRPC connected**, server validated my fake guid
3. `Target not allowed for this project` → server applied its policy

## Your correction was right on both counts

The HTTP transport has `subscribeEvents` = 0 refs, no `EventsResource`, no `HeartbeatHandler`. It cannot serve inbound. My "move everything to HTTP/V8" recommendation was wrong — gRPC stays for both directions. Docs corrected.

## The non-obvious thing that made it work

Convex installs an `externalPackages` entry **only if the bundled code imports it**. `nice-grpc`, `nice-grpc-common`, and `@grpc/grpc-js` are optional peers loaded *dynamically from inside* `advanced-imessage`, so nothing in the bundle references them — they're silently never installed, and `createGrpcClient` reports them missing even though they're in `package.json`.

The fix is a file nothing imports:

```ts
// convex/_workaround.ts
"use node";
export * as _grpcJs from "@grpc/grpc-js";
export * as _niceGrpc from "nice-grpc";
export * as _niceGrpcCommon from "nice-grpc-common";
```

A diagnostic action proved the flip: before, `import.meta.resolve("nice-grpc")` threw; after, it returned `file:///tmp/external_deps/.../node_modules/nice-grpc/lib/index.js`.

Also worth knowing: **`externalPackages` is ignored by the anonymous local backend** — that's why my earlier local test kept failing and I wrongly concluded gRPC was a dead end. Sends can only be tested on a cloud deployment.

## Two notes

I created a Convex project **`spectrum-convex-e2e`** (deployment `accurate-crow-731`) in your account, with the project secret set as an env var. Delete it when you're done, or keep it as a test bed.

Deployed. **Text it again** — it should be much faster and won't echo `[read]` anymore. Here's the measured breakdown of where those 11 seconds went:

## Whose problem: mostly mine, some Convex, a little Photon

Timing your `"1"` → `"echo: 1"` turn from the actual database rows:

| Stage | Time | Owner |
|---|---|---|
| You sent → webhook hit my endpoint | **1.57 s** | Photon (Spectrum Cloud delivery) |
| Debounce window | **5.01 s** | **Me** — `debounceMs: 5000` |
| Handler ran → send queued | 0.22 s | Me |
| Queued → delivered to iMessage | **4.69 s** | Me (pacing) + Convex cold start + gRPC |
| **Total** | **11.04 s** | |

The last row is the interesting one. Cold vs warm, from the outbox rows:

- **Cold** (first send): 4685 ms
- **Warm** (later sends): 1312–1744 ms, of which 800 ms was my own pacing → **~500–950 ms of real work**

So Convex's Node-action cold start costs ~3.5 s once per container; after that the module-level client cache does its job and gRPC round-trips are sub-second.

## Two real bugs, both mine

**1. Read receipts caused a feedback loop.** That `[read]` in your screenshot isn't cosmetic. The raw data shows: bot sends "echo: 1" → your phone auto-sends a read receipt → Spectrum delivers it as an inbound event → my component treated it as user input → new turn → echoed `[read]` → *that* got read → another receipt… It was echoing its own read receipts indefinitely.

Read receipts and typing indicators are now classified as signals: stored for visibility, but they never arm the debounce, never feed a batch, and — importantly — never cancel the turn they're acknowledging.

**2. Pacing delayed the first message.** `pacingMs` was applied to every send including the first, so it was a flat 800 ms tax on every reply rather than spacing between consecutive messages. Now the first send of a turn is never paced, and `markRead` never paces at all.

Plus `debounceMs` 5000 → 1200 in the example.

Expected total now: **~1.5 s (Photon) + 1.2 s (debounce) + ~0.7 s (warm send) ≈ 3.5 s**, down from 11 s — with the first message after an idle period still paying the cold start.

If you want it faster still, the debounce is the remaining dial — but it's the thing that makes bursts collapse into one reply, so dropping it to zero trades away the feature. Four regression tests added; 29/29 passing.

SigNoz changes the answer materially. **Most of the remaining latency is Photon's, not Convex's or mine.**

## Server-side p95, last hour, across your whole fleet

| Operation | p95 | Where |
|---|---|---|
| `grpc ChatService/MarkChatRead` | **2173 ms** | spectrum-imessage |
| `grpc MessageService/SendTextMessage` | **1184 ms** | spectrum-imessage |
| `inbound.deliver` | 257 ms | spectrum-imessage |
| `inbound.ingest` | 233 ms | spectrum-imessage |
| `binding.resolveInbound` | 79 ms | spectrum-imessage |

My measured "warm send ≈ 500–950 ms of real work" now has an explanation: `SendTextMessage` alone is **1.18 s p95 server-side**. My pipeline wasn't adding meaningful cost there — the gRPC call itself is slow.

And your own webhook traces for my endpoint (`b4050c5c…`):

- `webhook.deliver` to me: 212 / 305 / 172 / **496** ms
- The POST itself: 192 / 285 / 167 / **410** ms
- iMessage timestamp `06:28:24.083` → `webhook.deliver` start `06:28:25.520` = **1437 ms** before it ever left your side

## Corrected attribution of the 11 s

| Leg | Time | Owner |
|---|---|---|
| Apple → Mac → inbound pipeline → dispatch | ~1.44 s | Photon (~570 ms of it your own ingest/deliver/resolve) |
| Debounce | 5.00 s | **me** (now 1.2 s) |
| Webhook POST + my ack | ~0.19 s | me/Convex |
| Handler → outbox | ~0.22 s | me |
| Outbox → delivered (warm) | ~1.3 s | **~1.18 s is your `SendTextMessage`** |
| Cold start (first send only) | +3.4 s | Convex |

So the irreducible floor is **~2.6 s of Photon server time** per turn. Even with zero debounce and a warm container, that's the fastest this can go today.

**`MarkChatRead` at 2.17 s p95 is worth a look** — it's slower than sending a message, for what should be a trivial write.

## A bug in my own fix, caught by these numbers

Seeing markRead as a separate 2.17 s call made me re-read my pacing logic. I'd keyed "don't delay the first send" off `seq === 0` — but `markRead` occupies seq 0, so the actual reply landed in a *paced* slot and got the 600 ms delay anyway. It now counts message-bearing rows only; control actions don't consume a pacing slot. Test added, 30/30 passing, deployed.

## One thing I'd flag separately

Not latency, but it stood out: `fusor-fanin-imessage` is at **61.9 % error rate** (59,652 / 96,337 calls) and `codes.photon.spectrum-imessage` at **18.9 %** over the last hour. That's independent of this work — I didn't chase it since you asked about speed.

why is there a debounce window, remove that

It's from your own architecture docs — batching "hey" → "wait" → "actually" into one reply instead of three overlapping ones. But it's a fixed latency tax on *every* turn to solve a problem that only occurs in bursts, and the SigNoz numbers show something better: `SendTextMessage` takes ~1.2 s server-side, and a follow-up arriving in that window already cancels the pending send. Cancellation gives you burst collapsing for free.

They're my synthetic test messages — not real iMessages, and not from you.

I've been driving the pipeline with a script (`/tmp/burst.mjs`) that POSTs properly-signed webhooks straight at the Convex endpoint, simulating three messages arriving 400ms apart. `"hey"` → `"wait"` → `"actually — do trains run on holidays?"` is the canonical burst example from your own docs (`docs/best-practices/inbound-pipeline.mdx.vel`), so I reused it.

**The bug I just found is real regardless.** The mechanism doesn't care whether the messages are synthetic:

- `"hey"` arrives → chain 1 drains it → handler starts
- `"wait"` arrives → cancels chain 1, moves `"hey"` to the carry table
- chain 2 flushes → **deletes** `"hey"` from the carry table and hands it to the handler
- `"actually"` arrives → cancels chain 2 → only chain 2's *own* inbound rows carry forward

`"hey"` was already consumed from the carry table, so it's gone. The reply proves it: `echo (2 messages)` — it should have been 3.

Any real user typing three messages in quick succession loses the first one. Want me to go ahead with the fix? It's the same "drain in the handler, not the enqueuer" rule your docs already state, just applied to the carry table too: claim carried rows with the chain id instead of deleting them, release them on cancel, delete on completion.

content.text:
Debounce removed and a genuine data-loss bug fixed along the way. Both repos green: 37/37 component tests, 32/32 SDK test tasks, lint + typecheck + build clean.

## Why the debounce existed, and why it's gone

It batched bursts into one reply. But the SigNoz numbers showed a better mechanism was already there: `SendTextMessage` takes ~1.2 s server-side, and a follow-up arriving in that window already cancels the pending send. **Cancellation gives you burst collapsing for free** — no fixed tax on every turn. Default is now `0`; the knob remains if anyone wants stricter batching.

Live proof, three messages 272 ms apart:

```
echo (3 messages):
[Earlier] hey
[Earlier] wait
actually — trains on holidays?
```

One reply. Two intermediate replies queued and cancelled. No waiting period.

## The bug that removing it exposed

Your `"oh okay"` was well-timed, because the first burst test after removing the debounce dropped `"hey"` entirely — and it turned out to be **two** stacked defects, not one:

1. **Carried rows were deleted at flush.** A chain that inherited a message and was then superseded lost it, since it wasn't in `inbound` under that chain. Now claimed with the chain id and released on cancel.

2. **`completeChain` marked messages answered too early.** The handler finishing only means the reply is *queued*; a supersession moments later cancels it. So a message was marked answered while its answer never shipped.

Both collapse into one invariant, which the pipeline now enforces end to end:

> **A message is spent only when a reply actually reaches the user** — not when it's drained, not when the handler returns.

Carried rows are now discarded in `outbox.settle` on a confirmed send, not in `completeChain`. You can see it holding right now: the carry table still has `hey`/`wait` claimed by the surviving chain, because every send is bouncing off the target policy — nothing shipped, so nothing is discarded.

Six regression tests cover it, including back-to-back supersessions and the "already-sent, don't re-answer" direction.

## Worth noting

This bug was latent before, but harmless at `debounceMs: 5000` — the window was wide enough that supersessions rarely stacked. Dropping the debounce is what made it reachable. If you'd shipped the debounce removal without this, real users typing three quick messages would have silently lost the first.
dont do the message batching, are users of this component able to customize this behavior?

Straight answer: **no, not really.** `debounceMs` is the only knob — supersession, carry-forward, and batching are hardwired. That's a fair criticism of the design; an infrastructure component shouldn't impose one conversation policy.

Let me make it an explicit choice, defaulting to no batching:

```
webhook ──▶ verify + enqueue (durable) ──▶ 200
                     │
                     ├─ dedupe on message id (deliveries are at-least-once)
                     └─ start a turn
                                │
                                ▶ your onBatch handler
                                        │
                                        ▶ outbox ─▶ sender ─▶ iMessage
```

### Choosing a turn policy

The component does not impose a conversation model. Pick one with `mode`:

| `mode` | Behaviour | Use when |
|---|---|---|
| `"immediate"` *(default)* | Every message is handled on its own. N messages → N handler calls. `messages` always has one entry, `carried` is always empty. | Replies are cheap and answering each message is correct — echo bots, commands, notifications. |
| `"collapse"` | A burst becomes one turn. A new message supersedes the in-flight turn, cancels any reply that hasn't shipped, and carries its messages forward as prior context. | Replies are expensive (an LLM call), or answering each message separately would read as the agent talking over itself. |

```ts
new Spectrum(components.spectrum, {
  onBatch: internal.agent.respond,
  sender: internal.sender.deliver,
  mode: "collapse",   // default is "immediate"
  debounceMs: 0,      // optional extra settling window, collapse mode only
});
```

`debounceMs` is a latency cost on every reply, so it defaults to 0 — in
collapse mode, cancellation already absorbs most bursts on its own, because a
follow-up usually arrives while the previous reply is still in flight.

### Guarantees in both modes

- **At-least-once deliveries are deduped** on the provider message id.
- **Read receipts and typing indicators never start a turn.** Otherwise a bot
  replies to the read receipt for its own last message and echoes forever.
- **Sends are idempotent.** Each carries a `clientGuid` derived from
  `(chainId, seq)`, re-used verbatim on retry, so a send that landed before a
  lost acknowledgement can't post twice.
- **Messages are never dropped.** One rule governs the pipeline: *a message is
  spent only when a reply actually reaches the user* — not when it is drained,
  and not when the handler returns. A handler that has finished has only
  *queued* its reply; a follow-up moments later can still cancel it. Until a
  send is confirmed, every message stays recoverable. Verified live across two
  back-to-back supersessions.

content.text:
Batching is off by default, and it's now an explicit choice. Verified live — three messages produced three separate replies:

```
echo: hey
echo: wait
echo: actually — trains on holidays?
```

## Answering your question: previously no, now yes

`debounceMs` was the only knob. Supersession, carry-forward, and batching were hardwired — the component imposed one conversation model. That's now a documented option:

| `mode` | Behaviour | For |
|---|---|---|
| **`"immediate"`** *(new default)* | Each message handled on its own. N messages → N handler calls. `messages` always has one entry, `carried` always empty. | Cheap replies — echo bots, commands, notifications |
| `"collapse"` | Burst becomes one turn; supersedes in-flight replies and carries messages forward | Expensive replies (LLM calls), where answering each separately reads as talking over itself |

`debounceMs` is now meaningful only in collapse mode, and still defaults to 0.

## A bug this exposed in the first attempt

My initial immediate-mode implementation looked right and passed tests, but live it produced cancelled sends — which should be impossible when nothing supersedes.

Cause: all turns shared a single `inflight` row. Each new message's flush overwrote `chainId`, so `chainIsLive()` reported earlier turns as superseded and silently cancelled their queued replies. In collapse mode that's correct; in immediate mode, where several turns are legitimately open at once, it's wrong.

Fixed by giving each turn its own liveness record — a `chains` table, rather than inferring liveness from "is this the space's current chain?". That's more robust in both modes: it can't be confused by concurrent turns, and it's immune to two events landing in the same millisecond.

The unit tests missed it because they exercised one turn at a time. Added a regression test that opens three concurrent turns and asserts none invalidates another.

feat: Convex component for Spectrum iMessage

Convex cannot run Spectrum's `for await (… of app.messages)` loop, and
`app.webhook()` does not fit either: it dispatches its handler *after* the
HTTP response, but a Convex isolate is frozen the moment that response is
returned, so the handler would never finish.

This component inverts the order. A delivery is verified and written to a
table before the 200 is sent, so an acknowledged message is already durable;
everything after that runs on Convex's scheduler.

Inbound runs in the V8 runtime with no Node builtins — signature verification
uses `@spectrum-ts/core/webhook`, the portable slice of the SDK. Outbound
speaks gRPC from a Node action the app owns, because `"use node"` files may
only contain actions while the component is queries and mutations. It sits
behind a `Sender` interface so the transport can be swapped without touching
the schema or public API.

Turn policy is a choice rather than something imposed:

- `"immediate"` (default) — every message is handled on its own.
- `"collapse"` — a burst becomes one turn; a follow-up supersedes the
  in-flight turn, cancels any reply that has not shipped, and carries its
  messages forward as prior context.

One rule governs both modes: a message is spent only when a reply actually
reaches the user — not when it is drained, and not when the handler returns.
A handler that has finished has only *queued* its reply, and a follow-up
moments later can still cancel it, so until a send is confirmed every message
stays recoverable by the next turn.

Read receipts and typing indicators never start a turn; without that, a bot
replies to the read receipt for its own last message and echoes forever.

Verified end to end against a live Convex deployment and Spectrum Cloud:
signature rejection, at-least-once dedupe, per-message and collapsed turns,
back-to-back supersessions preserving every message, and gRPC sends reaching
Spectrum Cloud from a Node action.
EOF

I also dropped the `tsconfig.json` `paths` mapping, which pointed at my sibling SDK checkout and would have broken resolution for a cloner.

That's documented at the bottom of the README, and I made the CI workflow say so explicitly rather than implying green. I'd initially written a comment claiming the tests were independent of those subpaths — that was wrong (`wire.test.ts` imports them transitively), so I corrected it before committing.

content.text:
Here's everything sitting uncommitted in `spectrum-ts` — 13 files, ~140 changed lines plus 3 new ones. It splits into two shippable pieces and some docs.

## 1. Portable webhook verification — the load-bearing change

**`packages/core/src/webhook/verify.ts`** (+78/−~20) — rewritten on Web Crypto via `uncrypto`, so it now runs in a V8 isolate. Previously `node:crypto`, which Convex's default runtime doesn't have. It's now `async`.

Two behaviour changes beyond the swap:
- Strict hex decode — a malformed signature returns `signature-mismatch` instead of silently comparing a truncated buffer.
- An empty `secret` now throws instead of returning a 401-shaped result, since that's caller misconfiguration, not an unauthenticated request.

It also fixes a latent bug: `globalThis.crypto` isn't exposed by default on **Node 18**, which `@spectrum-ts/imessage` supports (`>=18.17`). uncrypto's conditional exports pick `node:crypto`'s webcrypto there.

**`packages/core/src/webhook/portable.ts`** (new, 36 lines) — the curated `@spectrum-ts/core/webhook` entry: `verifySpectrumSignature` plus the slim zod schemas. Deliberately excludes `deserialize.ts`, which drags in `node:fs`/`node:crypto` through the content builders.

**`packages/core/src/spectrum.ts`** — one line: `await` on the now-async verify.

Plus `package.json` (subpath export + `uncrypto` dep), `tsdown.config.ts` (build entry), and 12 tests updated to async with 2 added.

## 2. iMessage remote API export

**`packages/imessage/src/remote/entry.ts`** (new, 55 lines) — a curated `@spectrum-ts/imessage/remote` entry re-exporting the existing `remote/api.ts` verbs, `createCloudClients`/`disposeCloudAuth`, routing helpers, and attachment functions. **No new logic** — purely an export surface so a host that can't run the long-lived `Spectrum()` runtime can drive iMessage from its own scheduler.

Plus `package.json` and `tsdown.config.ts` wiring.

## 3. Docs and config

- **`docs/integrations/convex.mdx.vel`** (new, 191 lines) + a `nav.json` entry.
- **`biome.jsonc`** — two curated entry files added to the existing `noBarrelFile` exemption list, alongside `authoring.ts`.
- **`bun.lock`** — the `uncrypto` addition.

## Verification status

`bun run check`, `typecheck`, `test` (32/32 tasks), and `build` all pass. I confirmed with esbuild that `uncrypto` resolves to `globalThis.crypto` under `platform: browser` (Convex's V8 setting, zero `node:crypto` refs) and to `node:crypto` under `platform: node`, and that it stays an **external** import in the built chunk so the consumer's bundler picks the condition.

## Two things worth flagging

**Nothing here is Convex-specific.** Both subpaths are generic — the portable verify unlocks Cloudflare Workers, Vercel Edge, and Deno Deploy for webhook receipt too.

**There's a separate bug I found but didn't touch**, since it's outside this task: `cloud.getImessageInfo()`, `getPlatforms()`, and `getSubscription()` in `packages/core/src/utils/cloud.ts` don't send the `Authorization` header. All three fail with "Missing authorization header"; the same requests return 200 when I add Basic auth manually. One line each. Want me to fix that before you commit?

# Contributing to Spectrum

Thanks for your interest in contributing. This document covers how to set up your development environment, the expectations for contributions, and the workflow for getting changes merged.

## Code of Conduct

By participating in this project, you agree to abide by our [Code of Conduct](./CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md). Please report unacceptable behavior to the maintainers.

## Ways to Contribute

- **Report bugs** by [opening an issue](https://github.com/photon-hq/spectrum-ts/issues). Search existing issues first to avoid duplicates.
- **Suggest features** through GitHub Discussions or an issue describing the use case.
- **Improve documentation** — typos, clarifications, and new examples are always welcome.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/photon-hq/spectrum-ts.git
cd spectrum-ts
bun install

```bash
bun run build

bun run dev

bun run examples/basic/index.ts

```bash
bun run test            # whole suite under BOTH runtimes (via Turbo)
bun run test:node       # whole suite under Node only
bun run test:bun        # whole suite under the Bun runtime only
```
